theme: Walk about Zion, the city of God is secure
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 48. It is a song celebrating Jerusalem, “the city of our God.” Imagine walking around the walls and counting the towers, as the psalm invites you to do.
settingTheScene: Psalm 48 is a song of the sons of Korah. It follows Psalm 46 in this unit and in its original collection. The kings of the earth gathered against Zion, saw it, and fled in panic. It is the song of a city that has been delivered. You read it in Unit 9 as a song about the city of David. Today read it as the song of a city that has seen the Assyrian army vanish.
observation: “Great is the LORD and greatly to be praised in the city of our God! His holy mountain, beautiful in elevation, is the joy of all the earth” (vv. 1-2).
“Within her citadels God has made himself known as a fortress” (v. 3).
“For behold, the kings assembled; they came on together” (v. 4).
“As soon as they saw it, they were astounded; they were in panic; they took to flight” (v. 5).
“As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the LORD of hosts” (v. 8).
“We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple” (v. 9).
“Walk about Zion, go around her, number her towers, consider well her ramparts, go through her citadels” (vv. 12-13).
“That you may tell the next generation that this is God, our God forever and ever. He will guide us forever” (vv. 13-14).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with praise to the LORD and then to his city. The beauty of Zion is not the city for its own sake, but because of the God who lives there. The mountain is “the joy of all the earth,” and “the city of the great King.” In the ancient world, a city was only as good as its god. The psalmist insists that Jerusalem’s strength comes from its God.

The account of the enemies in verses 4 to 7 is brief and almost comic. The kings gathered, they came together, they saw, they were astounded, they fled. It is like a wave dissolving. Like “ships of Tarshish shattered by an east wind.” This is the same truth as Psalm 46 and Psalm 76: God defends his city.

Verse 9 is the center of the psalm. After the military story, the psalmist turns to the temple. “We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple.” The greatest thing about the deliverance is not the defeat of enemies but what it reveals about God’s covenant love. The people reflect on it in worship.

Then comes a strange invitation: “Walk about Zion, go around her, number her towers.” Walk the walls. Count what is still there. After a great threat, check that everything is intact. And the purpose: “that you may tell the next generation that this is God.” This is an educational walk. The visible city teaches children about God’s faithfulness. The final verse is a confession: “This is God, our God forever and ever. He will guide us forever.” The Hebrew can even be read “guide us beyond death.”

The psalm reminds us to remember what God has done and to pass it on.
connection: Matthew 5:35 calls Jerusalem “the city of the great King.” Hebrews 12:22 says that believers have come “to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.” Revelation 21:2 describes the new Jerusalem coming down from heaven, and verse 23 says it has no need of sun or moon, for the glory of God is its light. Matthew 16:18 says that the gates of hell will not prevail against the church. Deuteronomy 6:7 commands us to tell the next generation.
application:
Take a “walk about Zion.” List ten things God has done for your church or family, and number them like towers.

Tell a child, a new believer, or a friend one story of God’s faithfulness this week.

Think on God’s steadfast love, as the psalm says, during a time of worship.
prayerPrompts: Praise God for the security of his city.
Tell him what you have thought on of his steadfast love.
Ask him to guide you forever.
